newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Metals - Aluminium only interest in China.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Aluminium only interest in China.

text.p: Sporadic inquiries for aluminium ingots from Chinese trading companies are the only points of light in otherwise dark days for the base metals business in the Far East, traders said on Monday.

Theories abound for the lack of activity -- from greater competition leaving everyone a smaller slice of the China pie, to enough 1995 leftovers to keep Chinese consumers happy with a hand-to-mouth existence.
Aluminium ingot arrivals for October/November would be in the order of 5,000 to 10,000 tonnes, a European trader said, but this was not out of the ordinary.
"It's not a seasonal thing but China does need to maintain a certain level on the books of the domestic exchanges," he said.

Recent price dips on the London Metal Exchange (LME) had not been reflected on local Chinese exchanges, he said, where aluminium was trading around $1,660 a tonne, compared with around $2,650 at the start of 1996.
"The effect of the tremendous overstocking of 1995 continues and people are still living hand-to-mouth. As a result, they just got used to living off what they have," he said.
This had resulted in a slowing of Chinese aluminium exports to a trickle as more material stays at home, traders said.
Aluminium production for the whole of 1996 has been officially forecast at more than 1.8 million tonnes, 10 percent up on 1995's 1.65 million tonnes.
Imports in 1995 were 500,000 tonnes, with exports around half that, traders have said.

China's imports of unwrought aluminium and aluminium materials in the first seven months were 370,735 tonnes, up 26.1 percent on the same period last year, according to customs statistics. July imports of unwrought aluminium and aluminium materials were 71,836 tonnes, up from 53,395 tonnes in June, the figures show.
The European trader said the overall slowdown in the market would not be reflected in a dramatic drop in imports, but in drastically reduced exports.
Chinese aluminium output totalled 1.10 million tonnes in the first eight months of 1996, up by 1.34 percent compared with the same period of last year, the State Statistical Bureau said.
China's copper inquiries have dried up altogether, traders reported, as the LME price appeared volatile and no one wanted to get caught buying high with dips still to come.

Three month copper was indicated at $1,865/70 a tonne in early trade in London on Monday. Asian traders said sentiment in the red metal was still bearish and copper could slip towards $1,600 or even $1,300.

One said there was talk in the market that 100,000 tonnes of copper held in Shanghai bonded warehouses could be shipped back to LME warehouses and, if this were true, it would send copper on a further downward spiral.
Other traders said this was merely a rumour aimed at livening up a moribund market and had not been confirmed.
